summary: Defines a Timestamp Context Header for the Network Service Header, using the fixed-length metadata of MD Type 0x1. It carries the packet's timestamp, a sequence number, and a source interface identifier. The definition has not been standardized by the IETF but has been implemented, and is documented here for the community. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A small sticky note on each packet says when it was seen, its number, and where it came from.

subtitle: A common format for adding time, sequence, and interface data to NSH metadata.

tldr.problem: NSH allows fixed-length metadata (MD Type 0x1), but the NSH spec does not define what this metadata should contain or how services should use it. Multiple implementations were building incompatible formats.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a Timestamp Context Header that fills the 16-octet NSH metadata field with three items: a 32-bit sequence number (to detect lost or out-of-order packets), a 32-bit source interface ID (to identify which interface saw the packet), and a 64-bit timestamp (recording when the packet arrived).
tldr.outcome: The format was already implemented by multiple silicon manufacturers before IETF standardization. It is published as Informational to document a de-facto standard and improve interoperability in Service Function Chaining deployments.

facts.label: Fields
facts.value: Sequence Number (32 bits), Source Interface (32 bits), Timestamp (64 bits)

today: RFC 9192 is an Informational RFC published in February 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated. The Timestamp Context Header is implemented in silicon by multiple manufacturers and is deployed in Service Function Chaining environments for network analytics and performance monitoring.

sections.title: Adding Metadata to the Service Header
sections.content:
The Network Service Header (NSH) is a wrapper around packets in Service Function Chaining, an architecture where packets flow through a series of network functions. NSH includes a slot for metadata (MD)—extra information about the packet. The NSH spec [RFC8300] defines two ways to carry metadata: fixed-length (MD Type 0x1, 16 octets) and variable-length (MD Type 0x2).

The NSH specification does not say what the fixed-length metadata should contain. Several organizations proposed different formats for different uses (data center, broadband). This RFC defines one allocation—a Timestamp Context Header—that has already been implemented in silicon by multiple manufacturers. Publishing it standardizes an existing practice and lets different vendors' equipment work together.
sections.plainLanguage: Network packets flowing through service chains can carry sticky notes. This RFC says what should go on the sticky note when you want to add timestamps.

sections.title: The Timestamp Context Header Format
sections.content:
The Timestamp Context Header fills NSH's 16-octet fixed-length metadata with three fields. The first 4 octets hold a Sequence Number: a counter (starting at a random value on startup) that increments by 1 for each packet seen at the same source interface. Service functions can use this to detect lost packets or duplicates, though detection is only reliable when the same function instance processes the packet.

The next 4 octets are the Source Interface identifier: a number assigned by the classifier to identify the interface through which the packet entered. Combined with the classifier's identity, this uniquely identifies an entry point in the service chain.

The last 8 octets hold the Timestamp—when the classifier received the packet. The RFC allows two 64-bit timestamp formats: one based on IEEE 1588 (Precision Time Protocol, using seconds and nanoseconds) and one based on NTP (Network Time Protocol, using seconds and fractional seconds). Operators must choose one format and use it consistently across their domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The 16-octet stamp has three parts: a counter (to catch lost packets), an interface number (to know where it came from), and a timestamp (to know when it arrived). Each part is 4, 4, or 8 bytes.

sections.title: Using the Timestamp Data
sections.content:
The timestamp field can serve several purposes. Network analytics can use per-packet timestamps to measure coarse-grained delays across the service chain; if a delay spike is detected, a more detailed measurement tool can be triggered. Timestamps help with logging, troubleshooting, and flow analytics—for example, recording the timestamp of the first and last packet of a flow. Traffic mirroring and sampling applications benefit from a timestamp attached to each packet.

The Alternate-Marking method [RFC8321] for passive performance monitoring can reuse the timestamp; for instance, the least significant bit of the timestamp Seconds field alternates every second, providing a toggle marker for measuring packet loss and delay. Timestamp-based policies can enforce time-of-day policies or periodic actions in service functions—for example, 'trigger action A if timestamp >= T_0'. This enables consistent, coordinated network updates across the service chain.
sections.plainLanguage: The timestamp helps service functions measure delays, spot lost packets, and decide when to apply policies. For example, a service might temporarily drop traffic at a certain time of day using the timestamp to know when that time arrives.

sections.title: Clock Synchronization and Consistency
sections.content:
Many timestamp uses—especially analytics and performance monitoring—require classifiers and service functions to share a common time reference. Although not mandatory, most deployments using the Timestamp Context Header are expected to synchronize using the Network Time Protocol [RFC5905] or the Precision Time Protocol [IEEE1588].

The NSH specification does not forbid multiple MD Type 0x1 formats in one domain, but operators SHOULD ensure a consistent format is used. Specifically, they must agree on which of the two timestamp formats (IEEE 1588 or NTP) is in use, so all nodes interpret timestamps the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: For timestamps to make sense, devices need to agree on the current time—usually using NTP or a similar protocol. Within a network domain, everyone should use the same timestamp format (either IEEE 1588 or NTP style).

sections.title: Security and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
NSH typically operates within a single trusted domain, but in-band timestamping poses risks. An eavesdropper can use timestamped traffic to gather information about network delays and identify bottlenecks—a form of network reconnaissance. An attacker on the path can forge or modify timestamps to mislead performance-monitoring applications.

Timestamps depend on an underlying time synchronization protocol. If an attacker compromises the clock protocol (NTP or IEEE 1588), the integrity of the NSH timestamp is compromised. The RFC references [RFC7384] for a detailed discussion of time-protocol security. If the trust domain is insufficient, operators SHOULD use transport-level protection (TLS or similar) between SFC nodes, as described in RFC 8300.
sections.plainLanguage: Timestamps can leak information about how fast the network is, and a dishonest attacker could change timestamps to fool performance tools. Network operators need to protect the clocks and the links carrying timestamped packets.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: 32-bit counter per source interface; increments by 1 for each packet.

fields.name: Source Interface
fields.desc: 32-bit interface identifier; unique in context of the classifier.

fields.name: Timestamp
fields.desc: 64-bit time the classifier received the packet; IEEE 1588 or NTP format.
